raw_comment:
Putting a Price on Love
It was interesting to take a look at how much people spend on engagement rings, and how much of their salary they're spending on an engagement ring. The thing I’ve always heard about pricing for rings is that you are supposed to spend 2 months of your salary on an engagement ring. The graph has a significant drop off after about $3,000 dollars. There are of course outliers for the incredibly wealthy, with a spike in the data at 15,000+. But what really interests me is that the second lower graph shows that the people spending two months salary on an engagement ring are those who make less than 23,000. While anyone making more only spends around 2 weeks salary.  I wonder if that puts more strain on a poorer couples relationship, or if it means more because of the effort put into having enough to buy an engagement ring?

raw_comment:
I noticed that the information was different from logic's expectations. Usually, people with higher incomes would spend more on engagement rings since they have more money, while less well off consumers pay less. However, it was the complete opposite. Those with less than a $23,000 salary use 1/6 of their wages, while the highest income bracket of $90,000 spends 3.1%. I wonder if this is caused by hubris and humility. The latter might be arrogant and greedy, believing that they should keep most of their money and spend a little on a perceived small matter like engagement rings. On the other hand, those who can't live successful lives try to find other ways to live happily besides money, thus focusing on their partner. 

If I could create a catchy title for these two graphs, I would use "Engagement Rings Defy Logic!" This is due to the fact that while many believe it's important to have a significant other, the graph demonstrates that very little money is spent on it, and if a considerable amount is used, it is usually by people with low incomes.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of people buy rings that cost $500 dollars, as this is the biggest bar, and the majority of people don't by rings that cost more than 3k, as this is when there are no more than 50 people in each of the bars. I also noticed that although the lower chart shows that people in an income bracket above $23,000 spend a relatively similar percentage of their income on a ring, the price of the ring would continue to go up for every income bracket. 

In general it makes me wonder why engagement rings cost so much and why, as a society, we place so much value on engagement rings. Is it the product of capitalism and smart marketing tactics, or do people just want to show that they love someone so much they are willing to work so hard to give them an expensive ring?

raw_comment:
Engagement rings or engagement stings?
The number of owners is inversely proportional to the rise in the cost of rings, as there are fewer people who can afford expensive rings. Yet the number of rings shot up at the 15000 dollars sign, signaling that $15000 somehow confers the status of luxury and class. However, the average salary in the US is $56,516, which somewhat shows the striking income gap in America.
Another finding points out that while those who have less than $23000 of annual income spend a whopping 2.2 months worth of salary on an engagement ring, those who earn just a bit more ($23000 to $40000) spend only 2 weeks worth of income. The number of weeks continues to lower, but not on a significant margin as the annual income increases. Engagement stings much more when you are poor.

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  “Engagement Economy“ by Avery of Hoggard High School in Wilmington, North Carolina, “The Rings of Love Become the Rings of Pain" by Mohamed of Academy for Software Engineering, New York, “Engagement Rings, Hand Over 2 Weeks Salary” by Riley of Bush, and "The Price of a Promise" by Soren of Eden Prairie, Minnesota.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow --  Thursday afternoon, Feb. 13 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graphics, and a few Stat Nuggets.

The next graph will be released Friday, Feb. 21, with moderation on Wednesday, Feb. 26.  You may respond before, during, or after the live moderation by going to “What's Going On In This Graph?”  The topic --  contagious diseases.

You can see all of the released graphs on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” homepage.  Or, go to our post “Looking for Graphs to Use in the Classroom? Here Are 34.” for an index by context and an index by type of graph.

The link for the Stat Nuggets archives ishttps://tinyurl.com/StatNuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who is married and does not have an engagement ring, and Jen Mueller of St. Louis, who is married with an engagement ring.

raw_comment:
Headline: The Rings of Love become the Rings of Pain

I notice that 250 people in 2020 spend $1,000 or less on wedding rings. . People are spending lots of money in order to buy wedding rings that are taking up almost more than 2 and a half months of their income. This high spending makes it so that the wallets of the people buying are hurt due to the sheer amount of money they are willing to spend on wedding rings. Because of this, it's no wonder why people seek a cheaper alternative to this problem. I wonder what people do in order to fill in the gap of income money they have used. Do they work extra? Or maybe just pawn their rings? In my opinion I agree with the majority because the less money you spend, the more you can save it to really help you and your wife/husband's future.

raw_comment:
Headline: a diamond is forever, and so is the massive whole in your wallet. 
	
Looking at the graph I notice that a majority of people spend from 1 thousand to 15 thousand  dollars on engagement rings. That is a lot of money for a ring and think about how much practical stuff that you could get with fifteen thousand dollars. Then you also have to think about other wedding expenses like the venue, the dress, the suit, etc. in the end weddings can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.

My mom recently got engaged and her ring is definitely not on the cheaper side, this makes me wonder where she would be on this graph and how much all of these people end up spending overall on the wedding. 
Personally I would just be happy with a small cheap wedding. I think the union of two people doesn't need to be such a huge deal but in the society that we live in it is always made out to be this huge process when it doesn't need to be.
 I respect the group of people who spent less money on the engagement ring because they will probably be more fiscally responsible and it can help them later in life.

raw_comment: The most noticeable aspect of this graph is that the majority of the sample set spend from $1K-$3K on rings, while few spend from $10K-$15K. Additionally, those who earn less than $23,000 annually will spend 16.7% of this income on a ring, which is 2.2 months worth of their earnings. Individuals who earn more than $90,000 only spend 3.1% of their income, meaning that only 1.6 weeks of their earnings go towards the engagement ring. By taking a step back from the graphical data, a class divide is emphasized largely through the part of the graph illustrating the percentage of their income that is spent on an engagement ring. Lower middle-class and lower-class people can be significantly harmed due to this institutionalized cultural value of purchasing an expensive physical manifestation of one’s love for their partner. This possible harm towards one’s financial well-being causes these rings’ importance to be questioned. If there was another socially acceptable way to propose to a loved one that did not cause one to spend 16.7% of their income, would there be a small percentage decrease in the class divide or low-income levels? This graph illustrates how much an adult will spend on an engagement ring. The majority of the population sampled spends between $1K-$3K on a ring. This trend could reflect on how many Americans can not afford to spend more than that range of money on a single physical object, while very few make enough annually to spend $10K or more on an engagement ring.

raw_comment:
Headline: How to Ensure She Says Yes.

I notice that most people spend between 1K and 1.5K on an engagement ring. Once the prices get higher, the amount of people that spend that amount of money rapidly decreases. Therefore, the less the ring costs the more people that will buy that ring. The amount of money that one spends on a ring also depends on their income. The graph displays a wide range of money that one spends on money, as there is a 14K difference between the two extremes. 

I wonder if this graph just includes statistics from America.? If that is the case, I wonder what the graph would look like if it was a worldwide poll? Why the lowest income level has a higher-end limit in their range of money spent on the ring?

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph and map show the price people spend on engagement rings and how it relates to their income.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph and the map. 

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released on Friday, Feb. 21 (we're off for Presidents’ Week)  with moderation on Wednesday, Feb. 26.  The topic – the coronavirus and other contagious diseases.  Stay tuned.

raw_comment:
At first analysis of the provided graph from The New York Times, I noticed a graph that showed a decay or a depression. The graph compares the percentage of people from a study, and the amount the person spent on an engagement ring. The graph shows a prominent decay in the purchase of a ring as the price reaches an estimation of $2.5 thousand or $3 dollars. As the amount required to purchase the ring continues to increase the number of people willing to spend that amount decreases, which is until the final amount presented. At $15 thousand an increase of people that were able or even willing to purchase an engagement ring of that price.
	A more interesting aspect of the graph is the comparison of the annual income of an individual and the share of income spent on an engagement ring. The lower amount of income an individual made seemed to correlate how long they spent on either saving a ring or how long it would take to remake the amount they spend on a ring back. For example, an individual who made less than $23,000 a year would have to spend more than two months re-earning money back, whereas a person who made $23,000 to $40,000 would have to spend only two weeks.
	These graphs bring an interesting insight into the financial side of engagement rings and the financial impact they can have on an individual. While the meaning behind an engagement ring is typically more important than the financial worth, the impact of the cost is just as important as the meaning.

raw_comment:
In this graph, I notice that more than 250 people spend less than 1,000 on an engagement ring. Spending less than 1,000 on a ring is the most popular amount on an engagement ring. In addition, people with less than 23,000 annual income use 16.7% of their income which equates to 2.2 months of saving. I also notice how there is a severe decrease from a $3,000 ring to $10,000 and then a spike occurs around 15,000 again. This tells me that people usually purchase rings less than $4,000 but some will purchase a ring at about $15,000.  I wonder how much people spend on a wedding if their annual income is more than 90,000. I also wonder if adults spend more or less on wedding rings then they do engagement rings. 
TITLE: How Much Do People Truly Spend on an Engagement Ring?

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that most people spend a thousand dollars or less on engagement rings. I also noticed that the more expensive the engagement ring amounts to, the less likely people will buy it. I was able to surmise that when people have a meager income such as $23,000 or less, it takes them a little over 2 months to be able to afford the ring. On the other hand, if a person makes an annual income of $90,000 or more, they are able to buy the engagement ring in a little under 2 weeks. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder if  a person with a smaller annual income were to start saving for a more expensive ring far in advance, possibly a year, would they be more inclined to buy a more expensive ring or buy the cheaper ring?  I wonder about this because usually when a person has a smaller income they act more frugal with the money than someone with a larger annual income. People with a smaller income could likely be more inclined to make a more financial meager decision than the financial wealthy.

What do you think is going on in this graph?
The graph shows that when a person has a smaller income it takes up a larger share of their income that means they are probably going to be less likely to buy a more expensive ring. This means that if a person with  much larger income wants to buy an engagement ring, they will be more inclined to buy a more expensive ring because the cost of the ring would take up a smaller amount of the person's income.

raw_comment:
Engagement Economy

I have noticed a great difference in these costs. I see that a lot more people tend to spend somewhere in the $1,000-$3,000 range than anything else, and the amount spent steadily decreases from there. But, at the end, there is a small spike at the $15,000+ range. This part interests me. It seems that the standard and most affordable price is around $1,000-$1,500, and that is what most people pick because of their budget. As seen in the second graph, it is most common people spend around 1.6-2 weeks worth of their annual income on their engagement rings. But this brings me back to the spike in the $15,000+. This makes me wonder, is there a higher chance that people who are very wealthy throw the standard spending out the window and go berserk when buying their ring, and why would they spend that much on a ring?

raw_comment:
In a post by New York Times, there is shown a graph visualizing the relation of the cost of engagement rings to how many people buy them. Something of immediate notice on this article as a whole is that the date shows that the data was posted on the 12th of February, 2020, a time which has not yet come to New York. The most notable part of the graph itself is that, as far as the data on the graph shows, people buy more cheaper rings rather than expensive ones. Which is understandable, rings are expensive in general. What is interesting in this data, however, is the fact that after a steady decline in purchases as prices rise, there is a spike in the amount of people buying rings for $15k+.
	A question as to what the reason is for this data comes to mind after seeing the anomalies in this graph. Because as expensive as engagement rings already are in general, it would make sense that people should not buy as many expensive rings as much as cheaper ones. Especially when considering that engagement rings are separate from wedding rings, some people may want to spend more on wedding rings because they may simply mean more to both the givers and receivers. Yet after a cost of 15 thousand dollars per ring, people start buying again.

raw_comment:
Valentines has a nice Ring to it
I noticed that the most amount of people spent less than 1,000 dollars on their engagement ring. After 3,000 the graph significantly dips down  to show that less people are buying those more expensive rings. At the 15,000+ mark there is another dip back up.

I wonder why there is that dip back up at 15,000+ because I know that not that many people can afford that ring. It says that under 50 people had a ring at 15,000 or higher, and that's a lot for how many people were polled.

The graph starts out at the peak(250 people) and drops almost 50 people per 1,000 dollars spent until the graph reaches around 5,000. Then the graph becomes pretty stagnant until 15,000 where the numbers go up a small portion.

raw_comment:
First I notice that a plurality of people spend less than $1K Which… makes sense. However, it is a little interesting that it is not a majority. The second thing my eye is drawn too is the Huge discrepancy in portion of income, between people making less than 23,000 and everyone else.
  I suppose it's not surprising that the people that make the least play a larger portion of their income on engagement rings but what is fascinating how the discrepancy is set up. After you get out of the >$23000 bracket the rings portion of income almost Plateaus at 2 weeks. Where the lowest bracket is chilling at almost 2 months. Now this could be because engagement rings don't scale down to that low of income. It is also going to be affected more by extremes as the amount of starting money is already so low. Keep in mind this bracket could contain anyone making less than $23000. Which is where I have to believe the discrepancy is created. Look at all the following brackets, whose proportions are relatively even.
  I have sort of already mentioned it. I believe the > $23000 bracket is being raised most by people making much less than $23000. Such as a homeless man buying a ring with 8 months savings. Other than that the graph is pretty relaxed with proportion of income trending slightly down as income increases. The first graph does have a spike at the 15k+ price but that should be no surprise as the price includes the infinity above it. Those are the only considerable outliers.

I notice that more people choose to spend $1,000 to $3,000 on engagement rings. There is a drastic difference in the amount of people who buy engagement rings that are above $3,000. As the price goes up the demand for  more expensive wedding rings decreases along with the quantity. People with a lower income tend to save up for a longer amount of time to pay for the expenses of the engagement ring while it takes someone who has a higher income a shorter amount of time saving up.

The other graph shows that people who have a higher income are able to pay off the engagement ring a lot faster opposed to someone who has a lower income where they have to pay off the ring in a longer amount of time.

raw_comment:
1. I notice a trend in both graphs. The first graph has a very consistent trend. It starts off with more people buying cheaper rings, and as the ring price increases, the number of people decreases. Then at 15k there is a slight jump. On the second graph the trend is also pretty consistent. From $23,000 to $90,000 the amount of time spent is almost the same. And then at the less than $23,000 mark, the number jumps to something 4 times as much. Both graphs show common trends when it comes to money. The more money you have the more you can spend as well as the smaller period of time you have to save for.
2. I am wondering why there was a sudden jump when the first graph reached $15,000. The graph is fairly consistent until it reaches the very end. At the $15k the graph spikes and the current theory I have is that there are a very small percentage of people who are extremely rich and only they are able to spend that much. 
3. I think what is happening in the two graphs is that within the first one is that there are more people who earn small amounts of money and since the average price of an engagement is around that amount, more people are willing to pay that much. For the second graph I think that the people who earn more money are willing to save for similar periods of time. On the other hand, people who earn less are willing to save for longer because they have to save for longer to buy an averagely priced ring.

raw_comment:
More Money, Less Spent on Engagement Rings???

I found the survey was made up of 1,640 people, and the data was gathered in January. The graphs clearly show a trend of engagement ring costs peaking at the cheapest of under $500. Nevertheless, I wonder if the poll had more people and I'm curious if the chart would have been different in a later month near the tax cutoff. I also noticed those who made less money, often spent a greater percentage of income on the rings.
	I wonder why there was such a $15,000 spike on a ring relative to the ring that priced less but were still really costly. I wonder if this data can be used to evaluate the hard work and salary in different racial-economic classes. If these were based on different factors, such as race, gender, occupation, and age, would the graph trend the same way?
	Essentially, the lower amount of income a person generates, they are more likely to spend a greater percentage of their income on the engagement ring. This also enforces the common American ideal that you should put 1-3 months salary down on a ring, and is slowly disappearing for the middle to high class.

raw_comment:
I notice that there is a clear trend of more Americans opting to buy cheaper engagement rings. Due to the fact that Americans on the lower end of the income spectrum spend longer saving for an engagement ring, as shown in the second graph, numerous Americans are choosing to buy less expensive rings. Additionally, the income gap in the United States ensures that the vast majority of Americans are not able to spend an exorbitant amount of money on unnecessary items like engagement rings. 

I wonder why there is a spike in the number of people purchasing rings over $15,000.  I wonder why the group that makes $23,000 to $40,000 spends so much less time paying off their ring than the lowest income group. I also wonder what the average cost of a ring is for each income group. I think those added statistics would shed some light on exactly why each income group has the time frame that it does to save up for the ring. 

The graph overall shows the general trend of income that someone makes versus how much they spend on an engagement ring. There is a substantial drop-off after $3000, showing how Americans are generally spending a lower amount on engagement rings overall. This trend may be due to people making less money overall or people just choosing to save their money.

raw_comment:
There are several oddities with these graphs. In regards to the numbers, there were 1640 adults who participated in the survey. The majority of spenders paid less than five thousand dollars. A surprising amount of people who had an annual income of less than 23 thousand paid roughly 30 percent of that income on a ring. 
	My first thought is to wonder why lower income people spend such a large portion of their wages on a single time ring. I also wonder how these people compare to someone who spent proportionally less with the happiness and success of their marriage.
	The first graph shows the actual amount of a population spent on their engagement ring and the second graph shows the ratio of money spent to income earned. The less money that a person makes, the longer it will take for them to earn back the money they spent.

raw_comment:
The graph is presenting data about the price of engagement rings vs the number of people buying rings. The graph shows that people are spending less on engagement rings, but the trend is interrupted when the price of rings hits 15k. People of the lower income class tend to spend more of their income on rings, which shows the pressure in the United States to demonstrate your wealth. 
          I wonder why the number of people spending $15k on rings is so much higher than the price ranges before it. Also, why is it that people are spending less or around $1k for a ring, when before rings were used to show wealth. Is this graph showing that the US is moving away from showing wealth through material items, or is it just a coincidence that people are buying cheaper rings?
        The graph shows that people overall are buying cheaper rings, but there are outliers by the $15k range.  The chart under the graph also shows that people who earn less money spend much more of their income on rings than those who make more money. This is because a larger portion of their income has to go towards purchasing a ring than those who make more money on average.

In the first graph it is pretty consistent about the number of people buying rings that are more expensive being less. raw_comment:
When looking at the first graph, I noticed that the majority of people spend around $1k on engagement rings and I also noticed that at around $7.5k, the amount of people spending that much money drops significantly, but there is then a sudden surge of people at the $15k mark. I wonder if that surge of people towards the end occurs because the type of people who spend more than $7.5k are likely to have plenty of money to spare, so instead of just buying any other expensive ring, they just go all-in and buy an INSANELY expensive ring.  If that makes sense. I
     In the second graph, I notice that---based on the x and y axis values---rather than comparing the amount of people buying rings of various prices, it is comparing the percentage of someone's income that is spent on a ring in various annual income brackets. I wonder if this data could be used to analyze the dedication and commitment present in different socio-economic classes. Based on the graph, if it could be used in that way, then since people of lower income have more difficulty paying off their rings, and spend a large percentage of their earnings on it, then it can be assumed that they are more dedicated to their marriages. But obviously, this is a bold assumption and there are many other factors that come into play when determining the level of commitment present in a marriage, but it is fun to wonder if there is any sort of correlation there.
